issues.legal_issue: The prosecution must prove the accused’s guilt where the evidence of the alleged murder, ill-treatment, and dowry demands is unreliable or uncorroborated.
material_facts: The prosecution relied on relatives’ accounts and two alleged eyewitnesses, but the alleged eyewitnesses did not report the incident and their accounts were found unreliable.
The brother’s account of the deceased’s condition and the attempted objection to the cremation conflicted with other evidence, including an alleged eyewitness’s account of the cremation.
The father’s and brother’s accounts of dowry demands differed, and neither was corroborated; the sister did not support allegations of ill-treatment or dowry demands.
The letters written by the deceased did not complain of ill-treatment or dowry demands, and one described her circumstances at her marital home as good.
The High Court placed the burden on the accused to explain the death, although the prosecution had not established its case.
issues.conclusion: The prosecution failed to establish the appellants’ guilt; the convictions were set aside and the appellants were acquitted.
issues.legal_principle: The burden to establish guilt rests on the prosecution and, in the absence of a legal presumption, does not shift to the accused. The court applied this principle to the charges under Sections 302 and 34 of the Indian Penal Code. No earlier cases are cited for the principle.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_against_conviction and prosecution_witnesses_unreliable and (allegations_uncorroborated or correspondence_lacks_support_for_allegations) and prosecution_case_not_established

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_conviction: The accused appealed a conviction in a criminal case.
predicates.prosecution_witnesses_unreliable: The prosecution’s witnesses gave accounts that were unreliable or contradicted by other evidence.
predicates.allegations_uncorroborated: The allegations relied on to support the prosecution case lacked corroboration.
predicates.correspondence_lacks_support_for_allegat: Letters from the deceased did not support the allegations of ill-treatment or demands made against the accused.
predicates.prosecution_case_not_established: The prosecution evidence did not establish the accused’s guilt.

issues.definition: When an accused appeals a criminal conviction, unreliable prosecution witnesses and uncorroborated allegations, unsupported by the relevant correspondence, may leave the prosecution case unestablished, in which event the conviction cannot stand and acquittal follows.

issues.legal_issue: The Supreme Court may re-examine evidence despite concurrent judgments when the High Court’s approach to the evidence and the burden of proof is erroneous.
material_facts: Both courts below had convicted the appellants.
The High Court relied on the appellants’ failure to inform the deceased’s father and treated the accused as bearing the burden of explaining the death.
The Supreme Court considered that the High Court had overemphasized those circumstances and had misread the letters and other evidence.
issues.conclusion: Although the Supreme Court ordinarily does not examine facts minutely when the courts below have reached concurrent conclusions, the High Court’s erroneous approach justified re-examination of the evidence.
issues.legal_principle: The Court stated that it ordinarily does not go into questions of fact or examine evidence minutely when both courts below have given concurrent judgments, but may do so when circumstances such as an erroneous approach by the High Court warrant it. No provision or earlier case is cited for this principle.

predicates.criminal_appeal_with_concurrent_findings: The case is a criminal appeal in which the courts below reached concurrent findings.
predicates.high_court_used_erroneous_approach: The High Court’s assessment relied on an erroneous approach to the evidence or the burden of proof.

issues.definition: In a criminal appeal with concurrent findings, an erroneous approach by the High Court warrants Supreme Court re-examination of the evidence.
